title: Leaf Shape Explorer
description: Discover the incredible diversity of leaf shapes in your surroundings.
tasks: Find five leaves with distinctly different shapes — long, round, pointed, lobed, or heart-shaped
Gently feel the texture of each leaf — is it smooth, rough, fuzzy, or waxy?
Hold a leaf up to the sunlight and look at its veins — are they parallel or branching?
Look for a leaf that has been nibbled by an insect — nature's own artwork
observationTips: Compare leaves from the same tree — even on one branch, shapes can vary
Evergreen and deciduous plants have very different leaf textures
Some leaves smell distinctive when gently rubbed — try mint family plants
natureFacts: Leaves are green because chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light but reflects green
The world's largest leaf belongs to the raffia palm and can be over 25 meters long
A single mature oak tree can have over 200,000 leaves
reflectionQuestion: How many different leaf shapes exist within just a few steps of where you're standing?

title: Flower Detective
description: Investigate the fascinating structures and colors of flowers around you.
tasks: Find three flowers of different colors and observe them closely
Count the petals on each flower — is it 3, 4, 5, or many?
Look at the center of a flower — can you see the stamens or pistil?
Notice if any insects are visiting the flowers — they are pollinators at work
Gently smell each flower from a safe distance — how would you describe the scent?
observationTips: Flowers with strong scents often attract bees and butterflies
White or pale flowers are often pollinated by moths at night
Look for small flowers growing in cracks or at the base of walls
natureFacts: Sunflowers are actually made up of thousands of tiny individual flowers
Some flowers change color after pollination to signal to insects they are 'done'
The corpse flower can take 7-10 years to bloom just once
reflectionQuestion: What color or detail caught your eye that you usually walk past without noticing?
safetyReminder: Do not pick wildflowers — they support local ecosystems. Never eat or touch unfamiliar plants.

title: Tree Bark Investigator
description: Study the unique textures and patterns of tree bark in your area.
tasks: Find three trees with distinctly different bark textures
Touch each bark gently — describe the texture (smooth, rough, flaky, ridged, papery)
Look for any signs of life on the bark: lichens, moss, insects, or small plants
Estimate the circumference of the largest tree using your arm span
Look up into the canopy — how does the bark change from base to branches?
observationTips: Older trees usually have thicker, more deeply furrowed bark
Birch trees have distinctive white papery bark
Look for small holes in bark — they might be made by woodpeckers or beetles
natureFacts: Tree bark serves as armor, protecting against disease, insects, fire, and water loss
Cork comes from the bark of the cork oak tree, which can be harvested without killing the tree
Some trees shed bark regularly — it's a natural process of growth
reflectionQuestion: If you could describe one tree's bark to someone who has never touched a tree, what would you say?

title: Moss and Lichen Safari
description: Discover the miniature world of mosses and lichens growing on surfaces around you.
tasks: Find moss growing on a surface — a rock, a wall, a tree, or the ground
Look closely at the moss — can you see individual tiny stems and leaves?
Find a lichen — it may look like a flat, crusty, or leafy patch on a rock or tree
Notice the difference between moss (soft, green) and lichen (flat, often gray or yellow)
Check which direction the moss is growing — is there more on one side of a tree?
observationTips: Lichens are not single organisms — they are a partnership between a fungus and an alga
The old saying 'moss grows on the north side' is unreliable but fun to test
natureFacts: Mosses are among the oldest land plants, dating back over 450 million years
Lichens are used to monitor air quality — they are very sensitive to pollution
Some mosses can survive being completely dried out for months, then revive when water returns
reflectionQuestion: What did you discover by looking at things most people step over?
safetyReminder: Do not remove moss or lichen from surfaces — they are living organisms that support local ecosystems.

title: Wildflower Meadow Walk
description: Explore a grassy area to discover wild plants and meadow flowers.
tasks: Walk slowly through a grassy area, scanning the ground for small flowers
Find at least three different wildflowers or flowering weeds
Notice the variety of grasses — are they tall, short, feathery, or stiff?
Look for seed heads — dandelion clocks, grass seeds, or dried flower heads
Sit quietly for five minutes and notice how the plants move in the breeze
observationTips: Many 'weeds' are actually beautiful wildflowers — dandelions, clover, and buttercups
Look at the edges of paths and fences where wildflowers often grow
Spring and summer offer the most diversity, but autumn has seed heads and fall color
natureFacts: A single dandelion flower head is actually composed of up to 200 individual ray flowers
Clover enriches soil by converting nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use
Meadow grasses are some of the most important plants on Earth, feeding most of humanity through crops like wheat, rice, and corn
reflectionQuestion: What beauty did you find in plants that most people call 'weeds'?
